text: Foundations defined the steward role. A stewardship program is the operational machinery that makes that role actually function — and most stalled governance programs failed here, not at the role definition.

A steward almost always already has a job and takes this on in addition. Recruitment needs three things: the right person with deep domain knowledge, an explicit time allocation — commonly ten to twenty percent of their week, written down — and real buy-in from their manager that it won't get quietly absorbed by their primary job.

Stewards across domains face strikingly similar problems. A recurring peer forum — a community of practice — shares solutions so nobody solves the same problem alone, builds consistency across domains that would otherwise drift apart, and gives stewards a network that makes the role feel less isolated.

A program that never measures steward workload can't tell "stewardship is working" from "stewards are quietly falling behind." Track open issues per steward, time to resolution, and whether the negotiated time allocation still matches reality. When it doesn't, that's a signal to add stewards or time — not to expect them to absorb it.
Next lesson: once stewards and owners are in place, the full picture — roles, responsibilities, and how you actually onboard people into them.
